After a long shift, Jonas invites Mara to a café on Kastanienallee. The waitress comes over.
Hello! What would you like to drink?
I'd like a cappuccino and a water, please.
And I'll have a tea. Do you have peppermint tea?
No, unfortunately we don't have peppermint tea. But we have camomile tea or fruit tea.
Then a fruit tea, please. Without sugar.
Would you like something to eat as well?
Yes! I'll have the apple strudel. Mara, what are you having?
I'm not hungry. I won't eat anything, thanks.
What? After eight hours of work you're not hungry? I don't believe it!
Oh, all right… A piece of cheesecake, please. But not such a big one!
Together. Today it's on me, Mara. That's… fourteen euros sixty? Fifteen. Keep the change!
(you) would like; to like, to wish
“lade ein” = I invite, it's on me
“pf” is pronounced together, as a short, explosive “pf”: Pfefferminz, Apfel.
Käse is read “KAY-zeh”, with a long, open “e”.
After a vowel at the end of a word, the “r” almost disappears: “Bier” ≈ “BEE-uh”, “Wasser” ≈ “VAH-suh”.
“Möchten” is the polite way to ask for something. You use it in almost every order:
they would like; you (formal) would like
Careful: “er möchte”, without -t in the third person!
With another verb, the second verb goes to the END of the sentence, in the infinitive: “Was möchten Sie trinken?” “Ich möchte etwas essen.”

German has four cases. The first is the nominative (the subject). The second, the accusative, is for the direct object: what you take, what you drink, what you have. The good news: ONLY the masculine changes!
Verbs that take the accusative: haben, möchten, nehmen, essen, trinken, kaufen, brauchen, sehen. For example: “Ich habe einen Bruder” (chapter 2) was already accusative!
“Kein” negates a noun that would have “ein” or no article at all. It's declined like “ein”, but it also has a plural:
I have a brother. → I don't have a brother.
We have eggs. → We don't have any eggs.
“Nicht” negates everything else: verbs, adjectives, adverbs, nouns with a definite article or with a possessive:
Trick: if the positive sentence has “ein” or nothing before the noun → “kein”. Otherwise → “nicht”.
5. At the café and the restaurant
Tipping in Germany: you round the amount up and say the total out loud. For 14,60 € you say “Fünfzehn, bitte” or “Stimmt so” if you give 15. You don't leave the money on the table.
“Getrennt” is very normal in Germany: everyone pays their own share, even among friends.

It's Sunday, ten o'clock. Mara rings Mr Brandt's doorbell. Fritz is already barking.
The flat is small and old, but very cosy. Photos of trams hang on the wall.
On the table there are bread rolls, butter, jam, cheese, cold cuts and eggs. And a big pot of coffee.
Would you like a coffee, Ms Ionescu? With milk? With sugar?
With milk, but without sugar, please. Thank you!
Mr Brandt eats a bread roll with jam. Mara has an egg and a bread roll with cheese.
Fritz sits under the table. He wants something too. He wants the cold cuts.
No, Fritz! You're not getting any cold cuts. You're too fat!
Fritz isn't fat. Fritz is a dachshund. Dachshunds are long, not fat. That's what Fritz thinks.
Then Mr Brandt shows a photo: a young man in front of a yellow tram.
That's me. 1972. I was a tram driver for forty years. The M1 line, all through Prenzlauer Berg.
The M1! I take the M1 to work every day!
Mr Brandt smiles. He doesn't say anything. But he gives Fritz a little piece of cold cuts. Just a small one.
At twelve, Mara goes home. She's full and happy. Mr Brandt says: “Again next Sunday? At ten?” Mara says: “Gladly! But then I'll make breakfast. A Romanian one!”
